<h3 id="Warehouse-level-transaction-overview">Warehouse-level transaction overview¶</h3><p>Summarize observed sales and order volume by warehouse. Daily totals aggregate product records; missing warehouse-days are not filled with zero. Each product ID occurs in one warehouse only in this file, so the results support warehouse-level description but not same-product comparison across warehouses. Totals also reflect differing histories and product assortments. The notebook also reports a record-coverage proxy, where each product is considered active from its first through last observed date; this is a data-completeness diagnostic, not proof of assortment or stock availability.</p>

import numpy as np

# Confirm mapping and estimate daily record coverage against each product's observed active span.
product_warehouse_counts = df_clean.groupby("unique_id")["warehouse"].nunique()
print("Products assigned to multiple warehouses:", int((product_warehouse_counts > 1).sum()))
warehouse_daily = df_clean.groupby(["warehouse", "date"], as_index=False).agg(daily_sales=("sales", "sum"), sum_product_orders=("total_orders", "sum"), product_records=("unique_id", "nunique"))
warehouse_daily["active_product_count_proxy"] = 0
product_activity = (
    df_clean.groupby(["warehouse", "unique_id"])["date"]
    .agg(first_date="min", last_date="max")
    .reset_index()
)
for warehouse, daily_rows in warehouse_daily.groupby("warehouse"):
    activity = product_activity[product_activity["warehouse"] == warehouse]
    first_dates = np.sort(activity["first_date"].to_numpy(dtype="datetime64[ns]"))
    last_dates = np.sort(activity["last_date"].to_numpy(dtype="datetime64[ns]"))
    dates = daily_rows["date"].to_numpy(dtype="datetime64[ns]")
    active_counts = (
        np.searchsorted(first_dates, dates, side="right")
        - np.searchsorted(last_dates, dates, side="left")
    )
    warehouse_daily.loc[daily_rows.index, "active_product_count_proxy"] = active_counts
warehouse_daily["record_coverage_proxy"] = (
    warehouse_daily["product_records"]
    / warehouse_daily["active_product_count_proxy"].replace(0, np.nan)
)
warehouse_summary = warehouse_daily.groupby("warehouse").agg(observed_days=("date", "nunique"), first_date=("date", "min"), last_date=("date", "max"), total_sales=("daily_sales", "sum"), mean_sales_per_observed_day=("daily_sales", "mean"), summed_product_orders=("sum_product_orders", "sum"), mean_product_orders_per_observed_day=("sum_product_orders", "mean"), product_records=("product_records", "sum"), mean_record_coverage_proxy=("record_coverage_proxy", "mean"), days_at_least_99pct_coverage=("record_coverage_proxy", lambda s: int((s >= 0.99).sum())))
warehouse_summary["calendar_days_in_span"] = (warehouse_summary["last_date"] - warehouse_summary["first_date"]).dt.days + 1
warehouse_summary["missing_warehouse_dates"] = warehouse_summary["calendar_days_in_span"] - warehouse_summary["observed_days"]
warehouse_summary["unique_products"] = df_clean.groupby("warehouse")["unique_id"].nunique()
display(warehouse_summary.sort_values("total_sales", ascending=False).round(2))

from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error
import numpy as np

# Same forecast for all test dates
y_true = test_df["sales"].to_numpy()
y_pred = np.full(len(test_df), moving_average_forecast)

mae = mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)
rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))

# MAPE is undefined when actual sales are zero
nonzero_mask = y_true != 0
mape = np.mean(
    np.abs((y_true[nonzero_mask] - y_pred[nonzero_mask]) / y_true[nonzero_mask])
) * 100

print("Model: 7-day Moving Average Baseline")
print("MAE:", round(mae, 2))
print("RMSE:", round(rmse, 2))
print("MAPE (%):", round(mape, 2))
print("Test observations:", len(y_true))
print("Zero-sales observations excluded from MAPE:", int((~nonzero_mask).sum()))

from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error
import numpy as np

model = ExponentialSmoothing(
    train_df["sales"],
    trend=None,
    seasonal=None,
    initialization_method="estimated"
)

fitted_model = model.fit()

es_forecast = fitted_model.forecast(len(test_df))

y_true = test_df["sales"].to_numpy()
y_pred_es = np.asarray(es_forecast)

mae_es = mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred_es)
rmse_es = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred_es))

nonzero_mask = y_true != 0
mape_es = np.mean(
    np.abs(
        (y_true[nonzero_mask] - y_pred_es[nonzero_mask])
        / y_true[nonzero_mask]
    )
) * 100

print("Model: Simple Exponential Smoothing")
print("MAE:", round(mae_es, 2))
print("RMSE:", round(rmse_es, 2))
print("MAPE (%):", round(mape_es, 2))
print("Test observations:", len(y_true))

from scipy.stats import kruskal

weekday_groups = [
    group["sales"].values
    for _, group in product_df.groupby(
        product_df["date"].dt.dayofweek
    )
]

statistic, p_value = kruskal(*weekday_groups)

print("Kruskal-Wallis test")
print("Test statistic:", round(statistic, 3))
print("P-value:", round(p_value, 4))

if p_value < 0.05:
    print("Result: Sales distributions differ significantly across weekdays.")
else:
    print("Result: No statistically significant weekday difference detected.")

Kruskal-Wallis test
Test statistic: 24.488
P-value: 0.0004

<h2 id="4.-Weekday-Sales-Pattern-Analysis">4. Weekday Sales Pattern Analysis¶</h2><p>Average sales varied across the days of the week for product 4845. Thursday recorded the highest average sales (23.78), while Saturday recorded the lowest (19.53).</p> <p>The Kruskal–Wallis test indicated a statistically significant difference in sales distributions across weekdays (H = 24.488, p = 0.0004). This suggests that weekday related variation may be relevant to demand forecasting. Further validation is required before treating this pattern as stable weekly seasonality.</p>

# Build a calendar-day series so a 7-day lag means
# the same weekday in the previous week.
daily_sales = (
    product_df.set_index("date")["sales"]
    .sort_index()
    .asfreq("D")
)

# Keep missing dates as missing; do not treat them as zero.
daily_train = daily_sales.loc[:train_df["date"].max()]
daily_test = daily_sales.loc[test_df["date"].min():test_df["date"].max()]

# Seasonal-naive forecast: value from 7 calendar days earlier.
seasonal_naive_forecast = daily_sales.shift(7).reindex(daily_test.index)

# Evaluate only dates with both actual sales and a valid lagged forecast.
eval_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "actual": daily_test,
    "forecast": seasonal_naive_forecast
}).dropna()

mae_sn = mean_absolute_error(eval_df["actual"], eval_df["forecast"])
rmse_sn = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(eval_df["actual"], eval_df["forecast"]))

nonzero_mask = eval_df["actual"] != 0
mape_sn = np.mean(
    np.abs(
        (eval_df.loc[nonzero_mask, "actual"] -
         eval_df.loc[nonzero_mask, "forecast"]) /
        eval_df.loc[nonzero_mask, "actual"]
    )
) * 100

print("Model: Seasonal Naive (7-day lag)")
print("MAE:", round(mae_sn, 2))
print("RMSE:", round(rmse_sn, 2))
print("MAPE (%):", round(mape_sn, 2))
print("Evaluated observations:", len(eval_df))
print("Test dates excluded due to missing actual/lagged values:",
      len(daily_test) - len(eval_df))

from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose

# Use a continuous daily series, preserving missing values.
daily_sales = (
    product_df.set_index("date")["sales"]
    .sort_index()
    .asfreq("D")
)

# Fill missing dates only for this exploratory decomposition.

decomposition = seasonal_decompose(
    daily_interpolated,
    model="additive",
    period=7
)

decomposition.plot()

seasonal_component = decomposition.seasonal
residual_component = decomposition.resid

valid = pd.concat(
    [seasonal_component, residual_component],
    axis=1
).dropna()

seasonal_strength = max(
    0,
    1 - valid.iloc[:, 1].var() /
    (valid.iloc[:, 0].var() + valid.iloc[:, 1].var())
)

print("Estimated weekly seasonal strength:",
      round(seasonal_strength, 3))

eligible_products = product_summary[
    (product_summary["observations"] >= 365) &
    (product_summary["mean_sales"] > 0) &
    (product_summary["coefficient_of_variation"].notna())
].copy()

eligible_products["variability_group"] = pd.qcut(
    eligible_products["coefficient_of_variation"],
    q=3,
    labels=["Low variability", "Medium variability", "High variability"]
)

selected_products = pd.concat([
    group.sample(n=5, random_state=42)
    for _, group in eligible_products.groupby("variability_group", observed=True)
])

selected_products = selected_products.reset_index()

display(
    selected_products[
        [
            "unique_id",
            "observations",
            "mean_sales",
            "coefficient_of_variation",
            "variability_group"
        ]
    ].round(2)
)

<p>Handling Missing Dates</p> <p>The selected products contain some missing dates, ranging from 2 to 47 days. Since missing records do not necessarily indicate zero sales, the original observations are retained without automatically filling missing dates with zero values.</p>
In [39]:
gap_results = []

for product_id in final_product_ids:
    dates = (
        final_product_data.loc[
            final_product_data["unique_id"] == product_id, "date"
        ]
        .sort_values()
        .drop_duplicates()
    )

    full_dates = pd.date_range(dates.min(), dates.max(), freq="D")
    missing_dates = full_dates.difference(dates)

    if len(missing_dates) > 0:
        gap_series = pd.Series(missing_dates)
        gap_groups = gap_series.diff().dt.days.ne(1).cumsum()

        longest_gap = gap_series.groupby(gap_groups).size().max()
    else:
        longest_gap = 0

    gap_results.append({
        "unique_id": product_id,
        "missing_dates": len(missing_dates),
        "longest_consecutive_gap": longest_gap
    })

gap_summary = pd.DataFrame(gap_results).set_index("unique_id")
display(gap_summary)

from datetime import datetime

eval_product_ids = [
    product_id for product_id in final_product_ids
    if product_id != 3788
]

test_start = pd.Timestamp("2024-03-05")
test_end = pd.Timestamp("2024-06-02")

common_period_data = {}

for product_id in eval_product_ids:
    product_df = (
        final_product_data[
            final_product_data["unique_id"] == product_id
        ]
        .sort_values("date")
        .reset_index(drop=True)
    )

    train_df = product_df[product_df["date"] < test_start].copy()
    test_df = product_df[
        (product_df["date"] >= test_start) &
        (product_df["date"] <= test_end)
    ].copy()

    common_period_data[product_id] = {
        "train": train_df,
        "test": test_df
    }

    print(
        f"Product {product_id}: "
        f"Train = {len(train_df)}, "
        f"Test observations = {len(test_df)}, "
        f"Missing test dates = {90 - len(test_df)}"
    )

<p>Moving Average Forecast</p> <p>A 7-observation moving average was used as the baseline forecasting model. The average sales of the last seven training observations was used as the forecast for the testing period. Model performance was evaluated using MAE, RMSE and MAPE.</p>
In [42]:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error

baseline_results = []

for product_id, data in common_period_data.items():
    train_df = data["train"]
    test_df = data["test"]

    forecast_value = train_df["sales"].tail(7).mean()

    actual = test_df["sales"].to_numpy()
    predicted = np.full(len(actual), forecast_value)

    mae = mean_absolute_error(actual, predicted)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(actual, predicted))

    nonzero_mask = actual != 0
    mape = (
        np.mean(
            np.abs(
                (actual[nonzero_mask] - predicted[nonzero_mask])
                / actual[nonzero_mask]
            )
        ) * 100
        if nonzero_mask.any()
        else np.nan
    )

    baseline_results.append({
        "unique_id": product_id,
        "forecast_value": forecast_value,
        "test_observations": len(actual),
        "MAE": mae,
        "RMSE": rmse,
        "MAPE_percent": mape
    })

baseline_results_df = pd.DataFrame(baseline_results)

display(baseline_results_df.round(2))

from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import SimpleExpSmoothing

ses_results = []

for product_id, data in common_period_data.items():
    train_df = data["train"]
    test_df = data["test"]

    model = SimpleExpSmoothing(
        train_df["sales"].to_numpy(),
        initialization_method="estimated"
    ).fit()

    predictions = model.forecast(len(test_df))
    actual = test_df["sales"].to_numpy()

    mae = mean_absolute_error(actual, predictions)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(actual, predictions))

    nonzero_mask = actual != 0
    mape = (
        np.mean(
            np.abs(
                (actual[nonzero_mask] - predictions[nonzero_mask])
                / actual[nonzero_mask]
            )
        ) * 100
        if nonzero_mask.any()
        else np.nan
    )

    ses_results.append({
        "unique_id": product_id,
        "test_observations": len(actual),
        "MAE": mae,
        "RMSE": rmse,
        "MAPE_percent": mape
    })

ses_results_df = pd.DataFrame(ses_results)

display(ses_results_df.round(2))

from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import Holt

    model = Holt(
        train_df["sales"].to_numpy(),

    nonzero_mask = actual != 0

        if nonzero_mask.any()

    holt_results.append({
        "unique_id": product_id,

        "MAE": mae,
        "RMSE": rmse,

<h3 id="Comparison-of-Forecasting-Models">Comparison of Forecasting Models¶</h3><p>The three forecasting models were compared using MAE, RMSE and MAPE. Based on MAE, Holt’s Linear Trend model performed best for four products, Simple Exponential Smoothing performed best for two products, and the Moving Average model performed best for one product. These results indicate that forecasting performance varies across products and that no single model is consistently superior for all products.</p>

<h3 id="Aligning-Forecasts-with-Calendar-Dates">Aligning Forecasts with Calendar Dates¶</h3><p>Some products contain missing dates within the testing period. To maintain a consistent evaluation, forecasts should be aligned with the actual calendar dates rather than only the order of observed records. Missing sales values will remain unknown instead of being replaced with zero, since absent records do not necessarily indicate zero demand.</p>

<h3 id="Summary-of-Missing-Date-Validation">Summary of Missing-Date Validation¶</h3><p>Missing calendar dates were identified in both training and testing periods. <h3 id="Handling-Missing-Training-Values">Handling Missing Training Values¶</h3><p>For product 4067, the training data was converted to a daily time series. The two missing training values were estimated using time-based linear interpolation, while the testing data was left unchanged. This approach provides a continuous training series for the trial evaluation. Interpolated values are estimates and may differ from actual sales.</p>
In [64]:
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import (
    SimpleExpSmoothing, Holt
)
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error
import numpy as np

train_values = train_daily["sales"].to_numpy()
actual = test_df["sales"].to_numpy()
actual_dates = pd.DatetimeIndex(test_df["date"])
forecast_dates = pd.date_range(test_start, test_end, freq="D")
forecast_positions = forecast_dates.get_indexer(actual_dates)
if (forecast_positions < 0).any():
    raise ValueError("An observed test date falls outside the forecast calendar")
nonzero_mask = actual != 0

model_predictions = {
    "Moving Average": np.full(len(forecast_dates), train_daily["sales"].tail(7).mean()),
    "SES": SimpleExpSmoothing(
        train_values, initialization_method="estimated"
    ).fit().forecast(len(forecast_dates)),
    "Holt Trend": Holt(
        train_values, initialization_method="estimated"
    ).fit(optimized=True).forecast(len(forecast_dates))
}

model_predictions = {
    model_name: np.asarray(predictions)[forecast_positions]
    for model_name, predictions in model_predictions.items()
}

corrected_results = []

for model_name, predictions in model_predictions.items():
    corrected_results.append({
        "Model": model_name,
        "MAE": mean_absolute_error(actual, predictions),
        "RMSE": np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(actual, predictions)),
        "MAPE_percent": (
            np.mean(np.abs((actual[nonzero_mask] - np.asarray(predictions)[nonzero_mask]) / actual[nonzero_mask])) * 100
            if nonzero_mask.any() else np.nan
        ),
        "MAPE_observations": int(nonzero_mask.sum()),
        "Zero_actuals_excluded_from_MAPE": int((~nonzero_mask).sum())
    })

corrected_product_4067 = pd.DataFrame(corrected_results)
display(corrected_product_4067.round(2))

<h3 id="Comparison-Before-and-After-Missing-Value-Treatment">Comparison Before and After Missing-Value Treatment¶</h3><p>The original and corrected evaluations were compared across five products with complete test-period coverage. Missing training dates were handled by converting the training series to daily frequency and applying time-based linear interpolation, while the original test observations were retained.</p> <p>The overall metrics changed only slightly. The Moving Average results remained unchanged at two decimal places. Simple Exponential Smoothing showed a small increase in MAE and MAPE, while Holt’s Linear Trend model showed modest improvements in the three metrics. The overall ranking by evaluation metric remained broadly consistent: Moving Average achieved the lowest mean MAPE, and Holt’s Linear Trend model achieved the lowest mean RMSE. These findings apply to the selected products and should not be generalized to all e-commerce products.</p>
<h3 id="Forecasting-Methodology:-Fixed-Moving-Average-Baseline">Forecasting Methodology: Fixed Moving-Average Baseline¶</h3><p>The Moving Average model uses the average sales from the final seven observed training days to generate a constant forecast for the 90-day testing period. The forecast is not updated as new test-period observations become available. This approach serves as a simple baseline against which Simple Exponential Smoothing and Holt’s Linear Trend models are compared.</p> <p>Model performance is evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE).</p>
<h3 id="Scope-and-Limitations-of-the-Evaluation">Scope and Limitations of the Evaluation¶</h3><p>This study evaluates three forecasting methods—Moving Average, Simple Exponential Smoothing, and Holt’s Linear Trend—using five selected products from the Rohlik Sales Forecasting dataset. The products were selected based on data coverage, and the evaluation uses a common 90-day testing period from 5 March to 2 June 2024.</p> <p>Missing values in the training series were estimated using time-based linear interpolation, while the observed test data was retained unchanged. The Moving Average method uses the final seven training days to produce a fixed forecast. The models are evaluated using MAE, RMSE, and MAPE. MAPE excludes zero actual sales; corrected product tables report the observation count used and zero actuals excluded. Product IDs occur in one warehouse only, so product forecasts cannot compare the same product across warehouses. Warehouse totals are descriptive and reflect history length and assortment.</p> <p>The findings are limited to the selected products and evaluation period. The dataset does not directly measure inventory costs, stockout reduction, or business profitability. Therefore, the results indicate forecasting performance rather than proven improvements in inventory outcomes.</p>

<h3 id="Key-Findings-from-the-Forecasting-Analysis">Key Findings from the Forecasting Analysis¶</h3><p>The evaluation compared Moving Average, Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES), and Holt’s Linear Trend using five selected products over a common 90-day testing period.</p> <p>Holt’s Linear Trend achieved the lowest mean RMSE of 26.78, while its mean MAE was 20.85. The Moving Average model achieved the lowest mean MAPE of 32.35%. SES recorded a mean MAE of 20.85 and mean RMSE of 26.83.</p> <p>The results show that forecasting performance varies by evaluation metric and product. Although Holt’s Linear Trend performed well on absolute error measures, Moving Average produced the lowest average percentage error. The differences in mean MAE and RMSE were small.</p> <p>These findings suggest that simple forecasting methods can provide useful demand estimates for the selected products, but model choice should depend on the forecasting objective and the type of error that matters most. The results do not directly establish improvements in inventory costs, stock availability, or profitability.</p>

Holt’s Linear Trend achieved the lowest MAE for product 4067, while Simple Exponential Smoothing performed best for products 4425 and 4002. The Moving Average model performed best for product 2723. from scipy.stats import friedmanchisquare

friedman_stat, friedman_p = friedmanchisquare(
    complete_test_comparison["MAE_MA"],
    complete_test_comparison["MAE_SES"],
    complete_test_comparison["MAE_Holt"]
)

print(f"Friedman test statistic: {friedman_stat:.4f}")

if friedman_p < 0.05:
    print("Result: Statistically significant difference detected.")
else:
    print("Result: No statistically significant difference detected.")

Friedman test statistic: 0.4000
P-value: 0.8187

<h3 id="Statistical-Comparison-of-Forecasting-Models:-Friedman-Test">Statistical Comparison of Forecasting Models: Friedman Test¶</h3><p>A Friedman test was conducted to compare the MAE values of Moving Average, Simple Exponential Smoothing, and Holt’s Linear Trend across five selected products. The test produced a statistic of 0.4000 and a p-value of 0.8187. At the 5% significance level, the result was not statistically significant, so the null hypothesis was not rejected.</p> <p>The analysis did not identify sufficient statistical evidence that the forecasting methods differed in MAE across the selected products. However, the test was based on only five products, which limits its statistical power. Therefore, the result should not be interpreted as proof that the models perform equivalently.</p>

<h2 id="Expanded-Warehouse-Stratified-Rolling-Origin-Evaluation">Expanded Warehouse-Stratified Rolling-Origin Evaluation¶</h2><h3 id="Objective-and-evaluation-criteria">Objective and evaluation criteria¶</h3><p>This next-stage evaluation compares the 7-day Moving Average baseline, Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES), and Holt's linear trend across eligible product–warehouse series. Products are sampled within each warehouse and training-period coefficient-of-variation tertile, so the comparison covers different sales variability profiles. A product is eligible only when it has at least 365 observed training dates before 5 March 2024 and an observed record on every date in the shared 90-day evaluation window (5 March–2 June 2024).</p> <p>Use three expanding-window folds, each forecasting the next 30 calendar days. Missing training dates are interpolated by time within each fold; missing actuals are not filled and the sample requires full test coverage. MAE and RMSE use all actuals. MAPE excludes zero actuals, with included/excluded counts reported. Results are macro-averaged across product series so high-volume products do not dominate; warehouse results remain descriptive because products are not shared between warehouses. This is a single 90-day backtest, not proof of future operational benefit.</p>

# Build a reproducible warehouse- and variability-stratified sample for the shared test period.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

EVAL_START = pd.Timestamp("2024-03-05")
EVAL_END = pd.Timestamp("2024-06-02")
EVAL_DATES = pd.date_range(EVAL_START, EVAL_END, freq="D")
MIN_TRAIN_OBSERVATIONS = 365
MAX_PRODUCTS_PER_WAREHOUSE_VARIABILITY = 3
RANDOM_SEED = 42

# Group once rather than repeatedly scanning the multi-million-row source table.
eligibility_rows = []
for (warehouse_name, product_id), series in df_clean.groupby(["warehouse", "unique_id"], sort=False):
    series = series.sort_values("date")
    train = series.loc[series["date"] < EVAL_START]
    test = series.loc[series["date"].between(EVAL_START, EVAL_END)]
    observed_test_dates = pd.DatetimeIndex(test["date"].drop_duplicates())
    full_test_coverage = len(observed_test_dates) == len(EVAL_DATES) and observed_test_dates.equals(EVAL_DATES)
    if len(train) >= MIN_TRAIN_OBSERVATIONS and full_test_coverage:
        mean_sales = train["sales"].mean()
        std_sales = train["sales"].std()
        eligibility_rows.append({
            "warehouse": warehouse_name,
            "unique_id": product_id,
            "training_observations": len(train),
            "training_mean_sales": mean_sales,
            "training_cv": std_sales / mean_sales if mean_sales > 0 else np.nan,
            "test_observations": len(test)
        })

eligible_eval_products = pd.DataFrame(eligibility_rows)
if eligible_eval_products.empty:
    raise ValueError("No product series meet the training-history and complete-test coverage rules.")

# Rank first to make tertile assignment deterministic even when CV values tie.
eligible_eval_products["variability_group"] = ""
for warehouse, idx in eligible_eval_products.groupby("warehouse").groups.items():
    group = eligible_eval_products.loc[idx]
    if len(group) < 3:
        continue
    ranks = group["training_cv"].rank(method="first")
    eligible_eval_products.loc[idx, "variability_group"] = pd.qcut(
        ranks, q=3, labels=["Low variability", "Medium variability", "High variability"]
    ).astype(str).to_numpy()

# Exclude warehouses with too few eligible candidates to support the three variability strata.
stratifiable = eligible_eval_products.loc[eligible_eval_products["variability_group"] != ""].copy()
selected_eval_products = pd.concat([
    group.sample(
        n=min(MAX_PRODUCTS_PER_WAREHOUSE_VARIABILITY, len(group)),
        random_state=RANDOM_SEED
    )
    for _, group in stratifiable.groupby(["warehouse", "variability_group"], observed=True)
], ignore_index=True)
if selected_eval_products.empty:
    raise ValueError("No warehouse has enough eligible products for variability-stratified sampling.")

selection_summary = (
    selected_eval_products.groupby(["warehouse", "variability_group"], observed=True)
    .agg(products_selected=("unique_id", "count"),
         mean_training_observations=("training_observations", "mean"))
    .reset_index()
)
print("Eligible product-warehouse series:", len(eligible_eval_products))
print("Selected product-warehouse series:", len(selected_eval_products))
print("Warehouses represented:", selected_eval_products["warehouse"].nunique(), "of", df_clean["warehouse"].nunique())
display(selection_summary)
display(selected_eval_products.sort_values(["warehouse", "variability_group", "unique_id"]))

# Keep only the selected series for subsequent folds instead of repeatedly scanning all records.
selected_series_data = df_clean.merge(
    selected_eval_products[["warehouse", "unique_id"]],
    on=["warehouse", "unique_id"],
    how="inner"
)
selected_series_map = {
    key: group.set_index("date")["sales"].sort_index()
    for key, group in selected_series_data.groupby(["warehouse", "unique_id"], sort=False)
}

# Three expanding-window, 30-day folds; all model forecasts are aligned to calendar dates.
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import SimpleExpSmoothing, Holt

FOLD_DAYS = 30
fold_starts = [EVAL_START + pd.Timedelta(days=i * FOLD_DAYS) for i in range(3)]
model_names = ["Moving Average", "SES", "Holt Trend"]
fold_metric_rows = []

for item in selected_eval_products.itertuples(index=False):
    series = selected_series_map[(item.warehouse, item.unique_id)]

    for fold_number, fold_start in enumerate(fold_starts, start=1):
        fold_end = fold_start + pd.Timedelta(days=FOLD_DAYS - 1)
        observed_train = series.loc[series.index < fold_start]
        actual_series = series.reindex(pd.date_range(fold_start, fold_end, freq="D"))
        if actual_series.isna().any():
            raise ValueError(f"Missing actual test dates for product {item.unique_id}, fold {fold_number}.")

        train_daily = observed_train.asfreq("D")
        train_daily = train_daily.interpolate(method="time").ffill().bfill()
        train_values = train_daily.to_numpy(dtype=float)
        actual = actual_series.to_numpy(dtype=float)
        zero_mask = actual == 0
        predictions_by_model = {
            "Moving Average": np.full(FOLD_DAYS, train_daily.tail(7).mean()),
            "SES": SimpleExpSmoothing(
                train_values, initialization_method="estimated"
            ).fit().forecast(FOLD_DAYS),
            "Holt Trend": Holt(
                train_values, initialization_method="estimated"
            ).fit(optimized=True).forecast(FOLD_DAYS)
        }

        for model_name in model_names:
            predictions = np.asarray(predictions_by_model[model_name], dtype=float)
            nonzero = ~zero_mask
            fold_metric_rows.append({
                "warehouse": item.warehouse,
                "unique_id": item.unique_id,
                "variability_group": item.variability_group,
                "fold": fold_number,
                "fold_start": fold_start,
                "fold_end": fold_end,
                "Model": model_name,
                "MAE": mean_absolute_error(actual, predictions),
                "RMSE": np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(actual, predictions)),
                "MAPE_percent": (
                    np.mean(np.abs((actual[nonzero] - predictions[nonzero]) / actual[nonzero])) * 100
                    if nonzero.any() else np.nan
                ),
                "MAPE_observations": int(nonzero.sum()),
                "Zero_actuals_excluded_from_MAPE": int(zero_mask.sum())
            })

rolling_fold_results = pd.DataFrame(fold_metric_rows)
# Pool the equal-length folds within each series, then macro-average series.
def _aggregate_rolling_product_model(group):
    mape_counts = group["MAPE_observations"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    mape_values = group["MAPE_percent"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = np.isfinite(mape_values) & (mape_counts > 0)
    weighted_mape = float(np.average(mape_values[valid], weights=mape_counts[valid])) if valid.any() else np.nan
    return pd.Series({
        "MAE": group["MAE"].mean(),
        "RMSE": float(np.sqrt(np.mean(np.square(group["RMSE"].to_numpy(dtype=float))))),
        "MAPE_percent": weighted_mape,
        "MAPE_observations": group["MAPE_observations"].sum(),
        "Zero_actuals_excluded_from_MAPE": group["Zero_actuals_excluded_from_MAPE"].sum(),
        "folds_evaluated": group["fold"].nunique()
    })

product_model_scores = (
    rolling_fold_results.groupby(
        ["warehouse", "unique_id", "variability_group", "Model"], sort=False
    ).apply(_aggregate_rolling_product_model).reset_index()
)

warehouse_model_summary = (
    product_model_scores.groupby(["warehouse", "Model"], as_index=False)
    .agg(product_series=("unique_id", "nunique"),
         macro_MAE=("MAE", "mean"),
         macro_RMSE=("RMSE", "mean"),
         macro_MAPE_percent=("MAPE_percent", "mean"))
    .sort_values(["warehouse", "Model"])
)
overall_model_summary = (
    product_model_scores.groupby("Model", as_index=False)
    .agg(product_series=("unique_id", "nunique"),
         macro_MAE=("MAE", "mean"),
         macro_RMSE=("RMSE", "mean"),
         macro_MAPE_percent=("MAPE_percent", "mean"))
    .sort_values("macro_MAE")
)

print("Rolling-origin folds:", [(s.date(), (s + pd.Timedelta(days=29)).date()) for s in fold_starts])
print("Products evaluated:", selected_eval_products["unique_id"].nunique())
print("Per-product/model fold count:", rolling_fold_results.groupby(["unique_id", "Model"])["fold"].nunique().value_counts().to_dict())
print()
print("Overall macro-average (each product series equally weighted):")
display(overall_model_summary.round(2))
print()
print("Warehouse-level macro-average:")
display(warehouse_model_summary.round(2))
print()
print("Per-product model scores:")
display(product_model_scores.sort_values(["warehouse", "unique_id", "Model"]).round(2))

<h3 id="Interpreting-this-stage">Interpreting this stage¶</h3><p>Review the selected sample table first: confirm which warehouses and variability groups are represented, and note any underrepresented strata. Then compare overall and warehouse-level macro-averaged metrics, checking that each product has three folds. MAPE excludes zero-sales days; its counts are summed over folds. The score summaries are descriptive, and a model with the smallest average error is not automatically best for every warehouse or product. Treat this as an expanded, common-calendar backtest; it still does not model inventory availability, lead times, or stockout costs.</p>

<h2 id="Paired-Model-Comparison-and-Naive-Baseline">Paired Model Comparison and Naive Baseline¶</h2><p>This section adds a last-observation-carried-forward naive forecast to the same three 30-day folds used above. The naive value is the final daily training value after the notebook's existing time interpolation. It then compares all four methods on the same product–warehouse series. MAE is the primary paired comparison; RMSE is secondary. Friedman tests check for an overall difference, followed by paired Wilcoxon tests with Holm correction for the MAE pairwise comparisons. These tests are evidence about this sampled backtest only, not proof that models are equivalent or future performance is guaranteed.</p> <p>Run this cell after the expanded rolling-origin evaluation cell. It does not overwrite prior result tables.</p>

# Evaluate a last-observation-carried-forward naive forecast on the exact same folds.
# Then add paired, product-level tests; existing evaluation rows and outputs are preserved.
import itertools
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import friedmanchisquare, wilcoxon
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests

_required = {"warehouse", "unique_id", "variability_group", "Model", "MAE", "RMSE", "MAPE_percent"}
if "fold_metric_rows" not in globals() or not fold_metric_rows:
    raise RuntimeError("Run the expanded rolling-origin evaluation cell first; fold_metric_rows is unavailable.")

existing_folds = pd.DataFrame(fold_metric_rows)
_missing = _required.difference(existing_folds.columns)
if _missing:
    raise ValueError(f"Evaluation fold results are missing expected columns: {sorted(_missing)}")

naive_fold_rows = []
for item in selected_eval_products.itertuples(index=False):
    series = selected_series_map[(item.warehouse, item.unique_id)]
    for fold_number, fold_start in enumerate(fold_starts, start=1):
        fold_end = fold_start + pd.Timedelta(days=FOLD_DAYS - 1)
        observed_train = series.loc[series.index < fold_start]
        daily_train = observed_train.asfreq("D").interpolate(method="time").ffill().bfill()
        actual_series = series.reindex(pd.date_range(fold_start, fold_end, freq="D"))
        if actual_series.isna().any():
            raise ValueError(f"Missing actual test dates for product {item.unique_id}, fold {fold_number}.")

        actual = actual_series.to_numpy(dtype=float)
        prediction = np.full(len(actual), float(daily_train.iloc[-1]))
        abs_error = np.abs(actual - prediction)
        squared_error = (actual - prediction) ** 2
        nonzero = actual != 0
        naive_fold_rows.append({
            "warehouse": item.warehouse,
            "unique_id": item.unique_id,
            "variability_group": item.variability_group,
            "Model": "Naive (last value)",
            "fold": fold_number,
            "MAE": float(abs_error.mean()),
            "RMSE": float(np.sqrt(squared_error.mean())),
            "MAPE_percent": float((abs_error[nonzero] / np.abs(actual[nonzero])).mean() * 100) if nonzero.any() else np.nan,
            "MAPE_observations": int(nonzero.sum()),
            "Zero_actuals_excluded_from_MAPE": int((~nonzero).sum()),
        })

all_fold_results = pd.concat([existing_folds, pd.DataFrame(naive_fold_rows)], ignore_index=True, sort=False)

# Aggregate the three equal-length folds per product/model. Combining squared RMSEs
# yields the RMSE over the concatenated 90-day test period.
def _aggregate_product_model(group):
    mape_counts = group.get("MAPE_observations", pd.Series(np.ones(len(group)), index=group.index)).fillna(0).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    mape_values = group["MAPE_percent"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = np.isfinite(mape_values) & (mape_counts > 0)
    weighted_mape = float(np.average(mape_values[valid], weights=mape_counts[valid])) if valid.any() else np.nan
    return pd.Series({
        "MAE": group["MAE"].mean(),
        "RMSE": float(np.sqrt(np.mean(np.square(group["RMSE"].to_numpy(dtype=float))))),
        "MAPE_percent": weighted_mape,
        "folds_evaluated": len(group),
    })

baseline_product_model_scores = (
    all_fold_results.groupby(["warehouse", "unique_id", "variability_group", "Model"], sort=False)
    .apply(_aggregate_product_model)
    .reset_index()
)

print("Naive baseline rows:", len(naive_fold_rows), "(expected", len(selected_eval_products) * len(fold_starts), ")")
_complete_model_counts = baseline_product_model_scores.groupby(["warehouse", "unique_id"])["Model"].nunique()
print("Product series with all four models:", int(_complete_model_counts.eq(4).sum()), "of", len(_complete_model_counts))
display(baseline_product_model_scores.groupby("Model").agg(
    product_series=("unique_id", "nunique"),
    macro_MAE=("MAE", "mean"),
    macro_RMSE=("RMSE", "mean"),
    macro_MAPE_percent=("MAPE_percent", "mean"),
).sort_values("macro_MAE"))

# MAE is the prespecified primary paired outcome: each row is one product–warehouse series.
mae_wide = baseline_product_model_scores.pivot(index=["warehouse", "unique_id"], columns="Model", values="MAE")
model_order = ["Moving Average", "SES", "Holt Trend", "Naive (last value)"]
mae_wide = mae_wide.reindex(columns=model_order).dropna()
if len(mae_wide) < 3:
    raise ValueError("Too few complete paired product series for the planned tests.")

friedman_mae = friedmanchisquare(*(mae_wide[name].to_numpy() for name in model_order))
print(f"\nFriedman test across four models (primary MAE): n={len(mae_wide)}, statistic={friedman_mae.statistic:.4f}, p={friedman_mae.pvalue:.6g}")

pairwise_rows = []
for model_a, model_b in itertools.combinations(model_order, 2):
    differences = mae_wide[model_a].to_numpy() - mae_wide[model_b].to_numpy()
    if np.allclose(differences, 0):
        statistic, p_value = 0.0, 1.0
    else:
        result = wilcoxon(mae_wide[model_a], mae_wide[model_b], alternative="two-sided", method="auto")
        statistic, p_value = float(result.statistic), float(result.pvalue)
    pairwise_rows.append({
        "Model A": model_a,
        "Model B": model_b,
        "Median MAE difference (A-B)": float(np.median(differences)),
        "Wilcoxon statistic": statistic,
        "raw p-value": p_value,
    })
pairwise_results = pd.DataFrame(pairwise_rows)
pairwise_results["Holm-adjusted p-value"] = multipletests(pairwise_results["raw p-value"], method="holm")[1]
display(pairwise_results)

rmse_wide = baseline_product_model_scores.pivot(index=["warehouse", "unique_id"], columns="Model", values="RMSE").reindex(columns=model_order).dropna()
friedman_rmse = friedmanchisquare(*(rmse_wide[name].to_numpy() for name in model_order))
print(f"Secondary Friedman test across four models (RMSE): n={len(rmse_wide)}, statistic={friedman_rmse.statistic:.4f}, p={friedman_rmse.pvalue:.6g}")
print("Interpret lower MAE/RMSE as better. Treat these tests as sample-specific evidence; do not infer equivalence from a non-significant p-value.")

<h2 id="Warehouse-Level-Practical-Comparison">Warehouse-Level Practical Comparison¶</h2><p>This section summarizes the sampled product-series errors separately for each warehouse and estimates paired MAE differences against SES. Each product series receives equal weight. The bootstrap intervals resample product series within each warehouse; because only a small stratified sample was selected per warehouse, treat these intervals as descriptive uncertainty for this sample, not as proof of dataset-wide performance. A positive MAE reduction vs SES means the comparator has higher error than SES. No new significance claims are made here.</p>
In [82]:
# Requires the four-model product-level results from the paired comparison cell above.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

if "baseline_product_model_scores" not in globals():
    raise RuntimeError("Run the paired model comparison cell first.")

_scores = baseline_product_model_scores.copy()
_required_columns = {"warehouse", "unique_id", "Model", "MAE", "RMSE"}
_missing_columns = _required_columns.difference(_scores.columns)
if _missing_columns:
    raise ValueError(f"Product-level scores are missing columns: {sorted(_missing_columns)}")
if _scores.duplicated(["warehouse", "unique_id", "Model"]).any():
    raise ValueError("Expected one aggregated score per warehouse, product, and model.")

_model_order = ["SES", "Holt Trend", "Naive (last value)", "Moving Average"]
_warehouse_summary = (
    _scores.groupby(["warehouse", "Model"], as_index=False)
    .agg(product_series=("unique_id", "nunique"), macro_MAE=("MAE", "mean"), macro_RMSE=("RMSE", "mean"))
)
_warehouse_summary["Model"] = pd.Categorical(_warehouse_summary["Model"], categories=_model_order, ordered=True)
_warehouse_summary = _warehouse_summary.sort_values(["warehouse", "Model"])
print("Warehouse-level macro-average errors (products equally weighted):")
display(_warehouse_summary.round(2))

_mae_wide = _scores.pivot(index=["warehouse", "unique_id"], columns="Model", values="MAE")
if not set(_model_order).issubset(_mae_wide.columns):
    raise ValueError("Expected all four forecasting models in the results.")
_mae_wide = _mae_wide[_model_order].dropna()

# Descriptive paired differences: positive means SES has lower MAE than the comparator.
_rng = np.random.default_rng(2025)
_BOOTSTRAPS = 10000
_comparators = ["Holt Trend", "Naive (last value)", "Moving Average"]
_paired_rows = []
for warehouse_name, group in _mae_wide.groupby(level="warehouse", sort=True):
    for comparator in _comparators:
        ses_errors = group["SES"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        other_errors = group[comparator].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        differences = other_errors - ses_errors
        n = len(differences)
        bootstrap_means = np.empty(_BOOTSTRAPS, dtype=float)
        for b in range(_BOOTSTRAPS):
            bootstrap_means[b] = _rng.choice(differences, size=n, replace=True).mean()
        comparator_mean = float(other_errors.mean())
        reduction = float(differences.mean())
        _paired_rows.append({
            "warehouse": warehouse_name,
            "comparison": f"{comparator} minus SES",
            "product_series": n,
            "mean_MAE_reduction_vs_SES": reduction,
            "bootstrap_95pct_CI_low": float(np.quantile(bootstrap_means, 0.025)),
            "bootstrap_95pct_CI_high": float(np.quantile(bootstrap_means, 0.975)),
            "products_SES_lower_MAE_pct": float(np.mean(differences > 0) * 100),
            "reduction_pct_of_comparator_MAE": float(reduction / comparator_mean * 100) if comparator_mean else np.nan,
        })

_warehouse_paired = pd.DataFrame(_paired_rows)
print()
print("Paired MAE differences by warehouse (positive reduction favors SES):")
display(_warehouse_paired.round(2))

print()
print("Interpretation: use the warehouse table to describe where model errors differ. The paired reduction and bootstrap interval describe the selected products only; intervals overlapping zero indicate uncertainty about the direction in this small sample, not model equivalence.")
